## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_When does a tested machine have enough evidence to operate among people?_

A machine may complete its assigned task repeatedly while a premise behind its stopping distance remains untested. Granting it authority to operate requires deciding which claims the evidence supports, under which physical conditions, and for how long. That judgment connects the learned policy to the body, timing path, and independent permission mechanism on which each permitted action depends. Missing evidence can require a narrower operating envelope or a refusal, with the measurements needed to reconsider the decision stated explicitly. Evidence also ages as brakes wear, sensors shift, and software changes, so the release decision must remain tied to the running machine. At the causal boundary, authority must expire when its physical justification does, because a later software correction cannot undo motion already produced.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) safety case as an auditable engineering assertion DAG linking bounded operating envelopes to empirical hardware evidence
- Evaluate whether each claim's premises are measured, datasheet, illustrative, or unknown under the envelope trichotomy, and select the verdict they support
- Identify the exact hardware measurements that lift an operational refusal and the runtime contracts a conditional verdict maintains
- Specify standing conditions, decaying ODD micro-leases, and sensor calibration invariants that automatically withdraw motor authority via hardware watchdogs
- Diagnose unsupported warrants, hidden contextual assumptions, and compound defeaters through adversarial review of a release argument
- Design a cryptographically sealed safety case dossier and release manifest that bind upstream engineering contracts by digest and fail closed on any mismatch

:::

## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

The warehouse mobile manipulator must drive past rack ends, open a spring-latched cage door, and hand a ceramic mug to a coworker. Each task requires a different physical claim: sufficient stopping clearance, bounded latch force, or bounded handover contact. A successful run shows that the machine completed those tasks under the conditions encountered. A release decision must establish which conditions it may encounter next and which evidence supports operation there.

Verification has already stressed the machine's timing, bus contention, and sensor failure assumptions under injected faults (@sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection); what it hands over is its fault records, each evaluated against a predeclared pass-fail oracle, and the physical gaps they leave. The systems engineering task therefore shifts from finding individual software bugs to formally bounding what the empirical evidence licenses. Neither offline validation accuracy (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics) nor a run of clean demonstrations (@sec-verification-fault-injection) satisfies that requirement. Deciding to deploy is not a statistical prediction or an aggregate benchmark score; it is an auditable engineering adjudication of whether the physical evidence bounds the operational risk of the machine within a named operational design domain.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is produced in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

A deployment must also deliver useful service inside the supported envelope. The closed-loop task evidence of @sec-evaluation-logs establishes whether the policy completes the intended work, how often intervention interrupts it, and which conditions defeat it. Those results must be evaluated under the speed, payload, and site restrictions the release case can support. A machine that can only stop safely has not demonstrated useful task capability; a capable policy has not thereby justified actuator authority. The deployment decision joins both arguments for the same task and operating conditions.

The release case is scoped to service at one site. The signed fault records of @sec-verification-fault-manifest contribute evidence about particular failures, while clearance surveys, loaded stopping trials, and contact measurements support the physical criteria. The engineer must connect each record to the claim it supports and retain every premise the record leaves open.

A release verdict is a bounded, revocable engineering judgment. Its argument begins with the permitted operating envelope, links each physical claim to evidence, and determines whether full operation, restricted operation, or refusal follows. Standing conditions specify when that judgment expires. The worked adjudication and adversarial review test the argument before the release manifest carries its decision into the running machine; update and telemetry mechanisms must then preserve that connection.

## The Deployment Authorization Criterion {#sec-release-question}

At a rack end, the base must stop inside the available clearance. During handover, the arm must stay within the assessed contact-force limit. Both claims depend on the response arriving before its deadline. These requirements give release authorization testable physical criteria:
$$d_{\text{stop}}(v, \tau_{\text{delay}}, a_{\text{brake}}, \delta_{\text{loc}}, \epsilon_{\text{track}}) \le D_{\text{clear}}, \quad F_{\text{contact}}(v, m_{\text{eff}}, k_h) \le F_{\text{limit}}, \quad T_{\text{exec}} \le T_{\text{deadline}}.$$

Consequently, release authorization cannot rest on informal engineering intuition, anecdotal demonstrations, or aggregate benchmark metrics. It requires an auditable, machine-readable assurance argument that explicitly links high-level physical safety invariants to empirical sensor measurements, worst-case execution time bounds, and validated hardware fallback paths verified on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) regression benches before deployment. Furthermore, these physical criteria depend strictly on persistent hardware calibration parameters—including sensor extrinsic rotation and translation matrices ($[R \mid t]$), camera intrinsic matrices ($K$), joint zero-position encoder offsets, and actuator torque constants ($K_\tau$). Because these parameters represent individual physical machine traits rather than generic software weights, an embodied release framework must guarantee their retention and verification across Over-The-Air (OTA) updates; any parameter loss or uncharacterized calibration drift immediately invalidates the underlying kinodynamic stopping budgets.

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the release question is whether empirical evidence satisfies the physical criteria of each of its three collaborative tasks inside a scoped operational envelope: driving transit aisles without striking emerging pedestrians, opening a spring-latched door without exceeding mechanical structural limits, and handing a ceramic mug to a human coworker without exceeding biomechanical force limits. The release case names the certified physical bounds, the specified hardware fault model, and the validated permission and fallback ladder. It can support a revocable grant of tracking authority while those physical conditions hold; it cannot infer protection against uncharacterized or unmodeled hazards from finite test runs (\ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is the auditable, structured assurance argument for a specified physical machine, operating envelope, hazard criteria, and fault model, linking top-level safety claims to concrete empirical evidence through explicit engineering warrants.

1.  **Significance**: Transforms subjective, informal deployment confidence into an auditable, machine-readable engineering assertion Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)—implementing Compliance-as-Code—that connects top-level physical invariance claims to concrete empirical evidence across the entire cyber-physical stack.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike stateless software unit tests or static model validation scorecards, a physical safety case explicitly links operational design domain capability tokens, hardware fault-injection ledgers, sensor extrinsic calibration invariants, and deterministic runtime enforcer tripwires to demonstrate mathematically and physically bounded residual risk.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the safety case as a retrospective bureaucratic checklist completed after development, rather than an executable architectural contract that actively gates release manifests and runtime motor authority.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts, and
# │          the empirical-sufficiency probe of @sec-release-adversarial-review.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, the slow-downs before a takeover, and the
# │       restricted speed on inspected floors.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from calc_max_permitted_velocity with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads; mu_min = a_brake/g.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_mass, fmt_force, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_max_permitted_velocity, calc_c2_effective_deceleration

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
v_restricted = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors, the value @sec-frontier uses)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter / second)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(
    AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, calc_c2_effective_deceleration(a_inspected), overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin
).to(meter / second)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * RM.arm_effective_contact_mass) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.3898) < 5e-5, "Unconditional aisle speed ceiling is 1.39 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor is 0.204")
check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
check(mu_min > AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, "Inspected floor requires speed restriction")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.0947) < 5e-5, "Restricted ceiling on inspected floors is 1.09 m/s")
check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling, "Chosen restricted mode sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Coworker handover speed ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Running-machine loaded mass is 368 kg")
check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "In-loop takeover slow-down 1.2 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.3) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
check(AISLE.t_tick < AISLE.t_lease, "Servo tick sits inside the chunk lease")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is 50 kg")
check(
    abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
    "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseEnvelope:
    v_restricted = v_restricted  # chosen; read by calc-release-worked-verdict
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope, the target operational design domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain!release envelope} paired with the machine's own internal hardware, thermal, and timing invariants. In systems architecture, an ODD release is not a blanket or perpetual authorization; it operates as a set of decaying micro-leases—cryptographically scoped capability tokens with strict time-to-live (TTL) and hardware watchdog enforcement. An unconditional (`UNCOND`) verdict authorizes tracking proposals across the full verified operating envelope (@sec-verification-operating-envelope), a conditional (`COND`) verdict a named subset with restricted kinematics or environmental fences, and a refusal (`REFUSE`) none.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the operating envelope admits aisle travel at up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, on floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str`, past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. It admits door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and item handovers to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operational design domain and its known absences are defined in @sec-data-policy-coverage.
:::

Inside these boundaries the learned neural policy may propose actions across the nominal task envelope, but each action still requires independent, per-tick permission from an isolated safety enforcer. Conditional states of the monitored dimensions (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) narrow that envelope; for example, the machine slows to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before it requests an in-loop takeover. The restricted mode of a `COND` verdict narrows it further: on a floor known only through the site's inspection regime, the machine runs at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` inspected-floor ceiling.

As formalized in @tbl-16-odd-invariants, each monitored dimension is partitioned into nominal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$), conditional ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$), and refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$) intervals. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals via enforcer clamping. A refusal state revokes the capability token, withdraws motor tracking permission, and commands a validated fallback (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder). Crucially, on-board wheel slip estimation cannot provide prospective clearance guarantees: it detects low friction only *after* wheel slip has begun and traction is lost. A clear oil film ($\mu \approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) is optically transparent to camera sensors and visually indistinguishable from dry concrete. By the time a high-speed vehicle initiates braking on an oil patch and measures slip, it is already kinetically committed to an extended skid. Hence, floor friction must be enforced through site surveys and custodial spill regimes.

Sensor mounting drift can invalidate the localization allowance even when software remains unchanged; the mechanical mechanism is developed in @sec-release-calibration-drift. Release also requires **persistent hardware calibration parameter retention**\index{Hardware calibration!persistent parameter retention}\index{Over-the-air update!calibration retention}, so an update preserves the measured sensor transforms and joint offsets on which the case depends. The update process must verify those records before restoring tracking authority.

The evidence must also record what happens when operation reaches a boundary. **Edge event-triggered telemetry**\index{Edge telemetry!event-triggered buffer}\index{Black-box recorder!pre- and post-trigger capture} retains local traces for later review; the permission path enforces the live limits. The table lists the dimensions kept within bounds by runtime monitors or site procedures. Internal conditions from @sec-verification-operating-envelope, such as ambient temperature, rail voltage, and compute load, enter through the fault records trialed at them.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$)                                                                           | Conditional Boundary ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$)                                                                                                                                                        | Hard Refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$)                                                                                                                         | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before an in-loop takeover request; `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` before an out-of-loop one                                                    | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`)         | Inspection regime only ($\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): restricted `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\mu\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) is invisible to the cameras                                   | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le m\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`) | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                                                                               | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $D_{\text{clear}}\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                   | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                                                                         | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | None; demonstrations cover no other latch condition                                                                                                                                                         | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or displaced plate                                                                                                | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                                                                    | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or contact outside the assessed case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Each listed dimension has disjoint nominal, conditional, and refusal intervals. Conditional operation requires every dimension to remain in a signed admissible interval; missing or invalid measurements refuse. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

A defensible release claim states its plant, contact geometry, and fault set.[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] The machine's case uses three criteria. The base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before it reaches a person who has stepped out at a rack end, the arm opens the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit, and a handover never presses on the coworker with more than a chosen `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` peak force for an assessed contact case. The base's claim protects a stationary person; a person still walking toward the machine is a separate premise, carried by a site crossing rule (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). The release argument must demonstrate which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts the model covers, and which single faults the independent fallback handles. A stop after contact does not by itself cap the first force peak.[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Biomechanical Limits**\index{ISO/TS 15066!biomechanical limits}: The specification gives body-region- and contact-type-dependent force and pressure data [@isots15066]. A site assessment must select the applicable body region, contact geometry, and measurement procedure. The handover criterion used here is a conservative case criterion, not a universal ISO/TS 15066 threshold or an injury boundary.

[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]: **Contact Mechanics Force Model**\index{Contact mechanics!force model}: The elastodynamic model couples translational kinetic energy, effective moving inertia, and contact interface stiffness to determine transient peak impact force during an unmitigated collision. Impacting a rigid boundary concentrates stored kinetic energy into a sub-millisecond impulse with severe force amplification, whereas elastic compliance extends deformation time and dissipates energy over a longer stroke. For the formal elastodynamic derivation and unilateral contact formulations, see @sec-appendix-control-contact.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question, @eq-release-unbraked-force and the two
# │          paragraphs after it (spare spent as delay), and the refusal
# │          paragraph of @sec-release-three-verdicts (the deceleration the
# │          budget assumes).
# │ Goal: Show why the arm's handover speed is capped, and how little input
# │       error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: calc_transient_impact_force with the arm's effective contact mass and
# │      the coworker tissue stiffness; calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_c2_effective_deceleration,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass
f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(RM.tcp_speed_limit, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / AISLE.f_contact_criterion).to("dimensionless").magnitude
f_at_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * m_eff) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

c2_braking = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake)["distance"].to(meter)
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
t_spare = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
# Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance. The C2
# braking distance scales as 1/a, so a' = a_brake * d_C2(a_brake) / room.
braking_room = (AISLE.d_clear - AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay - overhead_loc - AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter)
a_break_even = (AISLE.a_brake * c2_braking / braking_room).to(meter / second**2)
a_shortfall_pct = ((AISLE.a_brake - a_break_even) / AISLE.a_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude * 100.0

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 424.26) < 0.01, "Unbraked force at the TCP limit")
check(abs(f_ratio - 8.49) < 0.01, "About 8.5x the 50 N criterion")
check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "Handover force is 42.4 N")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Handover ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "Spare spent as delay is 78.9 ms")
check(abs(a_shortfall_pct - 13.9) < 0.1, "A 14 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    k_h_str = fmt_stiffness(AISLE.k_contact_human, unit=newton / meter, precision=0, commas=True)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall_pct) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Consider the arm at its free-space speed limit of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str`, with a robot-side effective mass at the tool center point of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.m_eff_str`. In an unbraked elastic contact with the coworker's hand, modeled with an effective tissue stiffness $k_h$ of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.k_h_str`, the peak contact force follows @eq-release-unbraked-force:
$$F_{\text{unbraked}} = v\,\sqrt{k_h\,m_{\text{eff}}}$$ {#eq-release-unbraked-force}
This elastodynamic formulation derives directly from conservation of energy: equating translational kinetic energy ($\frac{1}{2}m_{\text{eff}} v^2$) to peak elastic strain energy ($\frac{1}{2}k_h x_{\max}^2$) stored in compressed human tissue at maximum deflection $x_{\max} = v\sqrt{m_{\text{eff}}/k_h}$, yielding peak contact force $F_{\text{unbraked}} = k_h x_{\max} = v\sqrt{k_h m_{\text{eff}}}$. In a sub-millisecond impact, unmitigated kinetic energy concentrates into an elastic impulse with severe peak force amplification.
At the free-space limit this ideal elastic model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str` the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion, so the arm cannot enter an unseparated contact at that speed without a stronger, measured protection argument. The same equation bounds the item-handover speed that the enforcement record caps (@sec-enforcement-telemetry, @sec-intervention-human-authority), since the criterion admits at most `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`. At the chosen `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str`, the model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`, inside the criterion.

The base's claim is a budget rather than a single force, and the delay components this chapter must evidence are the lease path and the observation age that its claims name. At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the finished budget (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget) is `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` against the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance, leaving a critical spare of only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`. That spare is the sole allowance for error across the entire perception-planning-actuation stack. An unbudgeted pipeline delay of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str` (the handover deadline $T_{\text{latest}}$ of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions) spends it entirely; so does a loaded deceleration shortfall of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes. Crucially, a sensor extrinsic calibration drift of just $\Delta\theta = 0.1^\circ$ creates a lateral perception error of $\Delta y = R \cdot \Delta\theta \approx 2.5\,\text{cm}$ at a scanning range of $R = 15\,\text{m}$, consuming over 24 percent of this entire stopping spare before active braking even begins. A stopping claim whose inputs are unmeasured cannot demonstrate that its spare survives these real-world compounding errors.

The release question for the mobile manipulator has become three bounded criteria: the base stops inside the clear distance, the arm opens the door under the latch limit, and an item handover stays under the contact criterion. Each calculation inherits premises about deceleration, latency, and contact stiffness that need physical evidence and can lapse in service. A safety case exposes those dependencies so a reviewer can decide which operating claims they support.

## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

A photograph of a clear aisle cannot establish that the loaded base stops inside it. That claim depends on clearance, braking capability, and response timing, each supported by evidence gathered under stated conditions. A safety case connects those premises to the claim so the release reviewer can identify what is supported and what remains untested.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_core.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the central causal core."}

*Release assurance: structured safety cases bounding the complete operational envelope across Sense, Plan, and Act.*
:::

### Assurance argument grammar and warrants {#sec-release-assurance-grammar}

The Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) safety case of \ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure} separates the proposition to be established from the reasoning and observations that support it. This organization draws on Stephen Toulmin's argument structure [@toulmin1958uses], Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)\index{Goal Structuring Notation}[^fn-std-gsn-argument] [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal], and the UL 4600 autonomy evaluation standard [@koopman2020how]. Its top-level claim $C_0$ names a testable physical property, such as keeping the base's stopping distance within surveyed clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) or limiting contact force ($F_{\text{contact}} \le F_{\text{limit}}$). Supporting claims identify the conditions needed for that result, and evidence records support those claims. Representing these links as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) makes their dependencies explicit: the reviewer can follow a claim toward its supporting observations without circular reasoning. The graph also records the operating assumptions under which each link holds.

[^fn-std-gsn-argument]: **Goal Structuring Notation**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!argumentation grammar}: Developed by Tim Kelly at the University of York, GSN provides an explicit graphical grammar for structuring and auditing safety assurance cases [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The notation decomposes top-level safety goals into contextual sub-claims, argumentation strategies, and solutions grounded in test artifacts.

The structural integrity of this engineering assertion DAG hinges on strictly distinguishing evidence from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!vs. evidence} is a record of successful task execution over an uncharacterized test distribution, such as a long run of clean door openings with the strike plate always at its nominal position or a thousand collision-free warehouse aisle transits. It measures mean performance but bounds neither the tail nor the failure modes outside the sampled trajectory. In contrast, evidence is a falsifiable, calibrated artifact with quantified uncertainty bounds, such as a worst-case execution time (WCET) distribution captured on a logic analyzer, loaded vehicle stopping trials across degraded friction regimes, or a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) fault-injection trace that drives the machine to the physical boundary of its envelope. An artifact without quantified uncertainty, or one that never stresses boundary conditions, remains an anecdotal demonstration and cannot support an inferential link in an engineering assertion DAG.

Connecting evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}, the inferential rule stating why the empirical data support the assertion. For a learned neural policy, the warrant is inductive, reasoning from failure-free test episodes to future operational reliability. However, the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits demonstrates why inductive warrants cannot carry a catastrophic hazard claim alone: under the Poisson zero-event rule ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), demonstrating an ultra-reliable failure rate ($10^{-9}$ per operating hour) would require billions of operating hours without a single incident. The safety case must therefore incorporate deterministic architectural warrants, grounding the top-level claim in an independent permission path (@sec-enforcement) that enforces Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to clamp actuator commands and command an assessed safe stop whenever a learned proposal approaches the boundary of the viable set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{viable}}$. That architectural warrant narrows the claim rather than escaping the exposure wall, since the permission path protects only against the specific hazards it monitors and can arrest within physical stopping limits (@sec-frontier-method-limits).

### Contextual assumptions and the weakest link {#sec-release-contextual-assumptions}

A stopping trial conducted in a well-lit aisle also depends on the sensing conditions there. Moving the same machine into a dim aisle can change observation age even when its brakes perform exactly as before. The argument must name such contextual assumptions so a valid measurement is not applied outside the conditions that give it meaning.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph).
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image, and what it would cost the aisle budget's spare
# │       if the age check did not refuse the frames.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (AISLE.perception_age), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase; spare from
# │      calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff, the constant deceleration
# │      whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_safe_stopping_distance, calc_c2_effective_deceleration

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
low_light_exposure_factor = 2.0  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: a dim aisle doubles the exposure)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_exp_nominal = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
t_exp_low = (low_light_exposure_factor * t_exp_nominal).to(millisecond)
dt_age = ((t_exp_low - t_exp_nominal) / 2).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
d_added = (AISLE.v_aisle * dt_age).to(millimeter)
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare = (AISLE.d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.101) < 5e-3, "About a tenth of the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseLowLight:
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

When an operating assumption remains unstated, it is guarded only by whatever secondary check happens to sit downstream in the execution pipeline. In the mobile manipulator's stopping budget, the warrant assumes that warehouse aisles maintain sufficient ambient illumination for the navigation camera's nominal exposure. Suppose a dim aisle doubles that exposure from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`. Because an image's age is timed from mid-exposure, each observation arrives `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older than the budget charges, which unchecked would carry the base another `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` at the `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, about `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` spare. The permission path's age check refuses those frames instead, and the base stops in an aisle the case assumed it could run. The team meets its lighting assumption as unexplained lost service, and only a check that the case never tied to lighting kept it from becoming a silent loss of clearance.

An assumption that no runtime check sees has no such backstop. Sensor mounting drift can introduce a spatial offset while every image still passes its age check. The case must name both the localization allowance and the evidence that keeps the physical sensor geometry within it. Treating fresh telemetry as sufficient evidence of correct geometry leaves that warrant unsupported.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Epistemic assumptions embedded within safety case warrants are critically interrogated in @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits.
:::

The weakest link governs every Claim-Argument-Evidence assertion DAG. In formal verification, the validity of a parent assertion evaluated over a conjunction of child sub-claims ($\bigwedge_{i} C_i$) is strictly bounded by the weakest leaf warrant. A safety case is not an aggregate scorecard where high performance in one branch compensates for a deficit in another. High accuracy on an object recognition benchmark does not offset an uncharacterized latency tail on the CAN-FD bus, nor does extensive policy simulation offset missing brake-wear data. If the base's stop decomposes into sub-claims for braking friction, thermal protection of the motor drives (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), and real-time trajectory bounding, a failed warrant in any single branch invalidates the root deployment claim. The systems adjudicator who reviews the case looks not for the volume of supporting artifacts, but for the single unevidenced leaf whose failure would permit physical harm.

### Argument-to-plant alignment and claim adjudication {#sec-release-argument-plant-alignment}

The warehouse machine's stopping calculation already names its brake onset, deceleration, and observation age. The release reviewer must determine which of those inputs has been measured on the proposed configuration. Correct arithmetic on illustrative inputs establishes a conditional result; it cannot establish that the physical machine satisfies the premises.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-claims
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SIX RELEASE CLAIMS ON THE RUNNING MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (scorecard lead-in) and
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard.
# │ Goal: Instance claims C1-C6 on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show: base budget at aisle speed against the clear distance; latch force at
# │       brake command, remaining compression, and the arm stop it requires;
# │       mug pick and handover speeds with the handover ceiling and force;
# │       renewal-to-onset time; enforcer WCET and deadline; friction needed
# │       for a_brake; observation age; the handover deadline T_latest at the
# │       in-loop takeover slow-down and at aisle speed.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; calc_safe_stopping_distance with the calc_c2_stop_suffix
# │      distance as an equivalent constant deceleration;
# │      calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation; calc_transient_impact_force.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_c2_effective_deceleration,
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: one warrant quantity per claim ────────────────────────────────
# C1 base: finished budget at aisle speed.
a_eff = calc_c2_effective_deceleration(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    millimeter
)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
# C1 door: force at brake command and the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
latch_stop = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
f_cmd = latch_stop["f_at_brake_onset"]
x_remaining = latch_stop["x_remaining"]
a_arm_needed = latch_stop["a_arm_needed"]
# C1 handover: unbraked elastic force at the handover speed.
f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, RM.arm_effective_contact_mass, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
# C2: last valid renewal to brake onset.
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
# C3: friction the credible deceleration needs.
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * RM.arm_effective_contact_mass) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)
# C6: an unacknowledged handover falls back by the spare spent as time, at the
# in-loop takeover slow-down (operative) and at aisle speed (a policy request).
t_timeout = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
budget_takeover = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
    AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin
).to(millimeter)
spare_takeover = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
t_latest_takeover = (spare_takeover / AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop).to(millisecond)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the table ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "C1 base budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(budget_aisle < AISLE.d_clear, "C1 budget fits inside the clear distance")
check(abs(f_cmd.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "C1 latch force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "C1 remaining compression 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "C1 arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "C1 handover force 42.4 N")
check(f_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion, "C1 handover force under the criterion")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "C2 renewal-to-onset 82 ms")
check(AISLE.enforcer_wcet < AISLE.enforcer_deadline < AISLE.t_tick, "C2 WCET < deadline < tick")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "C3 friction floor 0.204")
check(abs(AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, "C4 age 51.6 ms")
check(abs(t_timeout.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 78.9 ms at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 209.7) < 0.05, "C6 spare 209.7 mm at the 1.2 m/s slow-down")
check(abs(t_latest_takeover.magnitude - 174.7) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 174.7 ms at 1.2 m/s")
check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "C1 mug pick under the 1.0 m/s TCP limit")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "C1 handover ceiling 0.118 m/s")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseClaims:
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_timeout_str = fmt_latency(round(t_timeout.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_takeover_str = fmt_latency(round(t_latest_takeover.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
```

For the mobile manipulator's collaborative manipulation tasks, biomechanical limits inform the contact force case once the assertion names the contacted body region, pressure distribution, impact geometry, and measurement method [@isots15066]. The mobile base's claims, which constitute the core of the release argument, are structured directly from its empirical stopping distance budget and site survey records. Rather than relying on static paper certifications, the release architecture adapts functional safety and SOTIF methodologies [@iso26262; @iso21448] into an auditable engineering assertion DAG that decomposes random hardware faults from performance limits of intended function, verifying each leaf against concrete empirical test benches before gating runtime motor authority.

The claim-argument-evidence scorecard in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard states six claims and pairs each physical warrant with its adjudication on this book's evidence. The structural argument topology—decomposing claims into premises, evaluating adversarial defeaters, and deriving binding runtime contracts—is illustrated in @fig-16-cae-tree. Claim C3 shows the decision: an oil film can defeat braking traction, so nominal model accuracy cannot justify an unrestricted verdict. A physically realizable condition that invalidates a warrant in this way is its **defeater**\index{Defeaters!definition}, and @sec-release-adversarial-review turns the search for defeaters into a review method. Claim C6 stands only on the fault records that test the four authority rules @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over (A1–A4).

::: {#fig-16-cae-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) Claim-Argument-Evidence decomposition and defeater adjudication**: Hierarchical structure of safety claims for physical deployment. Claim C1 (Operational Safety: normal force $\le 50\text{ N}$) decomposes into sub-claims for tactile reflex (C1.1), secondary torque tripwire (C1.2), and deterministic execution latency (C1.3). An adversarial audit uncovers Defeater D1: residual cutting oil drops surface friction from $\mu = 0.85$ to $0.12$, causing silent slippage without elastomer strain. Because this defeats the primary tactile reflex and allows secondary impact force ($88\text{ N}$) to exceed the $50\text{ N}$ limit, unconditional release is REFUSED. Adjudication yields Conditional Operation only after binding runtime contracts are imposed: restricting payload mass ($m \le 1.5\text{ kg}$), mandating optical surface-dryness verification, and tightening the torque tripwire to $18\text{ N}$ to guarantee peak impact remains bounded ($F_{\text{peak}} = 38\text{ N} \le 50\text{ N}$)." fig-alt="Goal Structuring Notation tree showing Claim C1 decomposing into tactile reflex, torque tripwire, and deterministic execution. A red defeater box illustrates cutting oil dropping friction and defeating the reflex, causing Unconditional Release to be refused. : **Claim-argument-evidence review for the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Six claims and their adjudication on this book's evidence. A failed or unknown branch cannot be compensated by nominal model accuracy. {#tbl-16-cae-scorecard tbl-colwidths="[14,58,28]"}

::: {#chk-release-claim-argument-evidence-and-inductive-warrants .callout-checkpoint title="Safety case decomposition and warrants"}

Before presenting a safety case for adjudication, test its structure:

- [ ] **Top-level claim falsifiability**: Can you state the top-level claim as a falsifiable physical proposition, such as a stop inside the clear distance, rather than an aspiration?
- [ ] **Warrant validity**: Can you name the warrant connecting each test bench to the claim above it, and the premises under which that warrant holds?
- [ ] **Defeater enumeration**: Can you show where a defeater such as lens fouling or bus arbitration collisions appears in the argument graph?
- [ ] **Evidentiary provenance**: Can you trace every terminal evidence node to a signed test trace and a current calibration?
:::

The scorecard separates a physical requirement from the evidence available to support it. The release verdict must preserve that distinction across the whole case: a supported branch cannot compensate for a missing premise elsewhere.

## The Three Verdicts {#sec-release-three-verdicts}

Every row of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard ends in an adjudication, and the release decision resolves the whole assertion DAG into one of three verdicts: **unconditional operation**\index{Verdicts!unconditional operation}, **conditional operation**\index{Verdicts!conditional operation}, or **refusal to operate**\index{Verdicts!refusal to operate}. In systems architecture, these verdicts are not informal administrative labels or advisory certificates; they are cryptographically signed capability descriptors loaded into the real-time safety microcontroller before motor power stages are energized. The first verdict, unconditional operation (`UNCOND`), authorizes tracking proposals across the full operating envelope named in a signed release manifest while its standing conditions remain verified. Each hazard claim in that case requires empirical evidence for the specified physical plant, payload distribution, operational design domain, and fault set—with brake thermal capacity, stopping clearance, and tracking-error bounds qualified for that envelope (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), and independent permission checks wherever learned proposals can reach actuators (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary). The verdict does not eliminate residual or newly discovered hazards; it authorizes operation strictly under the assessed claims and mandates automatic revocation the instant their physical premises fail.

### Authorization boundaries and dynamic separation monitoring {#sec-release-verdicts-ssm}

The second verdict, conditional operation (`COND`), applies when empirical evidence demonstrates that the machine is provably safe within a restricted operating subset but lacks valid warrants for the full envelope. In hardware execution terms, `COND` acts as a cryptographic capability mask: it programs the safety microcontroller's memory-mapped parameter registers with restricted kinematic thresholds ($v_{\max} \le v_{\text{restricted}}$, $a_{\max} \le a_{\text{restricted}}$) and spatial geofences before motor gate drivers are energized. Whereas a conditional verdict (`COND`) is an offline, predeployment contract that permanently restricts the machine's operating envelope via cryptographic capability masking, a degraded mode is an online runtime fallback invoked when an active subsystem experiences transient loss of telemetry or sensor redundancy. Release then enforces physical, kinematic, or environmental boundaries that exclude unverified hazard states—such as de-rated joint velocities, a restricted illumination range, or a physical barrier that keeps humans outside the manipulator's workspace. Where contact force cannot be bounded for unseparated co-presence, a restricted case may require an assessed physical cell and validated access interlocks (@fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell), verified so the protective stop completes before a human can breach the hazardous volume.

::: {#fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Physical separation example**: A yellow industrial arm works behind yellow mesh fencing. Fencing can be one condition of a restricted release when a validated access interlock and stopping test support it. Source credit: U.S. Army Chemical Materials Activity / PEO ACWA." fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
![](images/jpg/fig16_real_robot_safety_cell.jpg){width="85%" fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
:::

While legacy industrial automation relies on static perimeter fencing (@fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell) governed by ISO 13855, collaborative physical AI systems replace rigid physical cages with dynamic **Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM)**\index{Speed and Separation Monitoring!ISO/TS 15066}\index{Safety separation distance!dynamic monitoring} under ISO/TS 15066. Rather than fixing a static boundary, the perception and permission stack continuously calculates the minimum protective separation distance $S_p(t_0)$ required between human coworkers and the machine via @eq-release-ssm-safety-distance:
$$S_p(t_0) = v_h (T_r + T_s) + v_r T_s + B$$ {#eq-release-ssm-safety-distance}
where:

- $S_p(t_0)$ is the dynamically evaluated protective separation distance at current time $t_0$;
- $v_h$ is the maximum expected human approach speed ($1.6\text{--}2.0\,\text{m/s}$ toward the hazard zone);
- $v_r$ is the robot's current directed velocity toward the human coworker;
- $T_r$ is the total system reaction latency ($t_{\text{sense}} + t_{\text{dma}} + t_{\text{enforce}}$), spanning optical exposure, DMA bus transfer across the SoC interconnect, and the deterministic safety enforcer tick;
- $T_s$ is the physical actuator stopping time under maximum commanded deceleration ($v_r / a_{\text{brake}}$);
- $B$ is a composite spatial safety margin ($B = \delta_{\text{loc}} + \epsilon_{\text{track}}$) combining sensor localization uncertainty $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ and the tracking error tube $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$.

When real-time perception detects that human separation has fallen below $S_p(t_0)$, the permission path revokes motion authority and executes a safety-rated stop. If the machine fails to maintain this separation—due to sensor latency $T_r$ exceeding its budget, coworker approach speed exceeding $v_h$, or actuator brake shortfall extending $T_s$—human transit closes the clearance gap before the machine can arrest its motion. Crucially, sensor extrinsic calibration drift directly inflates the spatial margin $B$: an unmonitored angular deflection of $\Delta\theta = 0.1^\circ$ at a scanning range of $R = 15\,\text{m}$ induces a lateral perception error of $\Delta y = R \cdot \Delta\theta \approx 2.5\,\text{cm}$, which directly expands $B$ and $S_p(t_0)$ by $25\,\text{mm}$. If the real-time enforcer does not dynamically account for this calibration drift, the machine under-calculates the required separation distance, converting a transient sensing deficit into severe physical trauma ($F_{\text{unbraked}}$, @eq-release-unbraked-force). For dynamic SSM to remain valid across operational lifecycles and software updates, camera extrinsics and joint zero offsets must be isolated within a protected, schema-versioned hardware calibration partition, ensuring that software changes never silently reset calibration constants to unverified defaults. Rather than segregating robots behind fixed steel barriers, dynamic SSM enables open-floor collaboration by continuously scaling admissible policy speed to the available stopping envelope.

Every condition attached to a release verdict is a binding contract, and each names a number the permission path enforces rather than the ceiling the physics allows. The item handover shows the difference. The contract signs a Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool Center Point!handover speed contract} speed below the ceiling that the contact criterion admits under @eq-release-unbraked-force, and the gap between the two speeds is the allowance for what the monitor cannot see at the instant it samples: speed growth between samples, encoder quantization error, and the drive's response to an enforcement clamp. A contract signed at the ceiling leaves no room for those terms, and the release case needs a measured bound on each before the signed speed can stand.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Deterministic fallback coverage supporting conditional release verdicts builds on @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder.
:::

The inspected-floor condition follows the same rule. Where the site's inspection regime certifies a friction coefficient of only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`, the credible deceleration falls to what that friction supports, and the budget that admits `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str` on surveyed floors admits only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str`. The contract binds only while its premises hold.

The third verdict, refusal to operate (`REFUSE`), is the mandatory outcome whenever the safety case contains missing warrants, uncharacterized tail latencies, incomplete fault-injection coverage, or unmonitored failure modes. For systems where kinetic energy removal causes harm (such as upright bipedal humanoids falling under gravity), `REFUSE` cannot simply drop motor currents to zero; it must mandate an assessed, powered descent or seated hold. If the enforcer's worst-case execution time under the placement's load has never been measured against its `{python} ReleaseClaims.deadline_str` deadline, or the fault set omitted the common-cause tests the placement names, the hazard remains unquantified and cannot support release. Refusal is likewise required when a physical measurement contradicts the model behind a budget term, such as loaded stopping trials that decelerate below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes.

A refusal verdict is an engineering deliverable, not an administrative failure. It moves a dispute between schedule and safety onto evidence by isolating the broken link in the assertion DAG. If release is refused because loaded stopping trials contradict the braking term, the team does not debate risk tolerance but repeats the trials at the loaded mass until the low tail of the deceleration is known, re-derives the stopping term from that tail, and returns for re-adjudication only when the aisle budget closes on the measured value. The refusal verdict defines the exact evidentiary test that must pass before re-adjudication can occur.

Accountability for the release decision must reside with an identifiable **lead systems adjudicator**\index{Lead systems adjudicator!accountability} rather than being diffused across development teams. When a vision team signs off on detection scores, an actuator supplier on torque curves, and a learning team on policy convergence, each assumes that another layer provides the margin. The adjudicator alone attests that the integrated system satisfies the safety case, and the attestation binds the verdict to a set of immutable technical artifacts, including the cryptographic hash of the verified policy weights, the calibration logs of the arm's contact-force sensing, the brake-onset trials together with a separately justified worst-response bound, and the stopping trials at the loaded mass that establish the credible deceleration. The adjudicator cryptographically signs the release manifest using an asymmetric private key anchored in hardware Root-of-Trust (RoT) silicon, committing personal and institutional accountability to the integrity of the evidence.

The adjudicator signs one of the three decisions in @tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy. A conditional verdict needs a separately evidenced restricted envelope; a known hole in the nominal argument cannot simply be relabeled as a safe restriction. No verdict moves the proposal boundary. Under `UNCOND` and `COND` alike the policy only proposes and the enforcer still admits each action, as principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} requires, so a release sets the envelope the permission path enforces and never grants the policy permission of its own.

| Signed verdict | Evidence required                                                                                                | Permission and runtime limits                                                                                                                                          | Expiry or refusal trigger                                       |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `UNCOND`       | Full operating-envelope claim, measured plant and timing bounds, independently validated permission and fallback | Policy proposes across full *signed* task envelope; every action passes the enforcer                                                                                   | Evidence, configuration, calibration, or standing premise fails |
| `COND`         | Restricted operating-envelope claim and its own evidence, limits, and fault coverage                             | Policy proposes only within signed reduced limits; every action passes the enforcer                                                                                    | Any restricted premise becomes false or unknown                 |
| `REFUSE`       | Missing, contradictory, expired, or unauthenticated critical evidence                                            | No autonomous tracking permit; execute the assessed stop or hold, the fallback-ladder rung the release case validates for the plant (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder) | Re-adjudication with repaired evidence                          |

: **Three signed release verdicts for the mobile manipulator**: Full operation and restricted mode both retain independent per-action permission. Refusal is an actionable engineering result. {#tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[14,32,32,22]"}

### Mechanical degradation and thermal calibration drift {#sec-release-calibration-drift}

None of the three verdicts is a permanent grant. Mechanical linkages develop backlash, friction surfaces wear, lenses accumulate dust, and ambient distributions change, so operating under `UNCOND` or `COND` carries obligations for the life of the deployment. Brake wear that lowers the loaded deceleration by the shortfall that spends the aisle budget's spare (@sec-release-question) leaves the budget no allowance for any other input error. That wear must fail a standing condition (a scheduled stopping trial or a validated brake self-test) before the machine re-enters the aisle, since a stop in service would first reveal it at a rack end. Each such obligation pairs a premise with a detector and a response, which makes it one of the standing conditions the verdict carries.

A critical example of physical degradation that invalidates a release verdict is sensor extrinsic calibration drift\index{Calibration drift!thermal and vibrational mechanics}. In operating environments, diurnal thermal swings ($20^\circ\text{C} \to 45^\circ\text{C}$) cause uneven thermal expansion ($\Delta L = \alpha L \Delta T$) of aluminum chassis rails and sensor brackets, while floor-induced vibrational shocks continuously relax fastener preloads. An unmonitored angular deflection of just $\Delta\theta \approx 0.1^\circ$ in a camera or lidar mount produces a lateral spatial error of $\Delta y = R \cdot \Delta\theta \approx 2.5\,\text{cm}$ at an obstacle scanning range of $R = 15\,\text{m}$. In a warehouse aisle, this $2.5\,\text{cm}$ perception error consumes over half of the entire localization allocation ($\delta_{\text{loc}} = 40\,\text{mm}$), corrupting the robot's spatial transform tree (URDF / tf2 frame graph) and silently invalidating collision-avoidance guarantees without triggering any neural out-of-distribution detection.

Because software rollbacks, weight fine-tuning, or container restarts cannot correct physical bracket deflection or mechanical fastener relaxation, release manifests must establish continuous online extrinsic calibration tracking (such as multi-sensor bundle adjustment residual monitoring) and mandatory physical recalibration intervals as non-negotiable standing conditions.

## The Verdict's Standing Conditions {#sec-release-standing-conditions}

Brake wear can invalidate a stopping claim while the signed software remains unchanged. Standing conditions keep the release tied to such physical premises by specifying when each is checked and what happens when it fails. Their observation schedules follow the failure mechanism rather than the software release cycle.

### The envelope trichotomy and epistemic gaps {#sec-release-envelope-trichotomy-sub}

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-standing-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STANDING PREMISES OF THE MACHINE'S RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-standing-conditions (opening paragraph and the
# │          envelope-membership paragraph).
# │ Goal: Tie the standing conditions to the premises the machine's claims use.
# │ Show: friction needed for a_brake against dry concrete, tote-rack capacity,
# │       and the base tracking bound.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; mu_min = a_brake / g. The permission rail's hold-up
# │      is sized in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder; the manifest only signs it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_mass, fmt_length, check

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
```
